title: Chapter 186 – Han's Offer
html:
[The Valley Wall, Gate Tower – Head Han]

The granary of the Azure Cloud Sect is the size of a hill, and Han has spent the better part of a week arguing with her own sums.

She stands on its threshold at dawn with Lu Fei at her elbow and a lantern in her fist, looking down the long stone ramp into the dark. The air is dry and sweet and faintly dusty. Rows of great clay jars, each taller than a man, stretch away into the gloom, sealed with wax and stamped with the Sect's cloud-sigil. Beyond them, stacked to the vault, are the sacks. Rice. Millet. Barley. Dried beans. Pressed tea. Salt fish in oiled paper. It is, by any measure, a fortune.

"Thirty-one thousand measures," says Lu Fei. He is holding a tally-board. His thin ink-stained fingers have not stopped trembling since the Wall. "Counted at midnight. Allowing for rot and the rats."

"And the Sect?"

"Two thousand, eight hundred and eighty-six pupils. Plus servants, plus the wounded, plus the families of the Outer Court."

"Winter?"

"At full rations, ninety days leaves us with a surplus of nine thousand. At half rations, perhaps fourteen." He hesitates. "If we give nothing away."

Han does not answer. She stands in the cold dry breath of the granary with the lantern throwing her shadow huge across the jars, and thinks about the number she has not let herself say aloud.

One thousand, nine hundred and twelve.

That is how many pupils have died. It is the figure on the black board in the Gate tower, in her own hand, with the names in a column beneath. It began as seven hundred and twelve. It became seven hundred and thirteen. Then the third night came, and the fourth, and the long grinding dawn of the fifth, and the number climbed past a thousand, and she stopped being able to write the names down in order, and began to write them in the order that she remembered them.

Gu is on the list. He is the eighth hundred and something. She does not know the exact number. She has never asked.

"Head," says Lu Fei. "There is a letter."

"Whose?"

"From the Garden. By pigeon, at the fourth hour." He holds it out. "It is not an appeal. I thought you would want to see it."

She takes it. It is a single slip of pale paper in Zhao's hard upright hand, and it says, without salutation: We have taken in nine hundred and forty-three. Our grain is sixty days short. We do not ask. We tell you only that we will be hungry, and that we thought you should know.

Han reads it twice.

Then she folds it, very small, and puts it inside her robe, against the place where the old pain sits.

"Call the Elders," she says.

* * *

Lu Fei lays out the problem on the map table before the Elders come, and it is worse than she thought.

He has spread the readings in nine long strips of paper, one for each section, each marked with the small neat crosses of a week's observations. The Weights hang from a frame above them, swaying faintly. He does not look up as she enters. He is tracing a line with the end of his brush, and his lips are moving.

"Section one," he says. "Steady. Held by the Garden guard and the second rotation. Section two, steady. Section three..." The brush stops. "Section three has dropped eleven in four days. It was at seventy. It is now at fifty-nine. At this rate it fails by midwinter."

"The same limestone?"

"The same. The footing is hollow, Head. The whole Pass is honeycombed. We built on a shelf of soft stone eleven centuries ago because the Founders told us to, and I think they knew what was underneath." He taps a second strip. "Five is worse. Five has a void forty feet across. Seven, eight, they follow. Nine is the only one we have mended, and we mended it with a man."

She stares at the strips.

"How many keystones?" she says.

"For a full repair? Six, at the minimum." His voice is quiet. "I have thought about alternatives. Stone plugs. Pressure sleeves. A cradle of iron beams. None would hold. The array needs a will to stand on. Gu understood that. It is why he chose it." He rubs his eyes with a hand. "I do not think the Sect can pay six more Gus, Head."

"No."

"We would have no Elders left."

"I know." She is silent a moment. "Is there any other way? A way to give the array a will without a life?"

"There is one." Lu Fei hesitates. "In the old records. A name. The Founders' charter speaks of a Keeper, a person of sufficient stature, whose name could be written into the array as a second key. The living man does not have to give his life. He only has to give his name, and walk the Wall."

"The Keeper of Walls."

"Yes." He blinks at her. "You have heard of it?"

"I have heard of nothing else," says Han, "since the sixth night."

* * *

The Gate tower council chamber is a long bare room with a table of black ash and twelve chairs, and tonight eleven of them are filled.

The twelfth is Gu's. It stands at the table's foot, pushed back, empty. Nobody has taken it. Nobody has sat near it. A bowl of cold tea stands before it, untouched, with a faded heron on its rim.

Han takes her own chair at the head. She does not sit at once. She stands with her hands flat on the wood and looks down the table, at the faces. Elder Shan, the youngest, thirty-eight, round-eyed and anxious, who has not slept since the Wall. Elder Ro, the archivist, whose beard has gone gray in a week. Elder Pei, who lost her left hand to a crawler and has not yet stopped trying to use it. Elder Mu, at her right, lean and stern and seventy, with a face like a hatchet and the cold clear eyes of a man who has never been wrong about a thing he cared about.

She gives them the numbers. She gives them the letter. She gives them, because she has promised herself she will be honest, her own conclusion.

"I propose we give them twelve thousand measures."

There is a silence.

It is not the silence she expected. It is not shock. It is something more careful, more watchful, the silence of eleven people each deciding how to say no.

"Twelve thousand," says Elder Mu.

"A little more than a third of our stores."

"Which would leave us with nineteen. For two thousand, eight hundred and eighty-six pupils, plus servants, plus wounded." Mu's voice is dry. "At half rations, that is sixty days. After that, we eat the Outer Court's goat."

"We would eat the same bowls as they."

"We would eat the same bowls as a clan that has historically despised us."

"Mu."

"I do not say it from malice, Head." The old Elder lifts a hand. "I say it as a matter of record. For forty years, the Lin clan has treated the Sect as a bank and a landlord and an irritation. They paid their tithes late. They slighted our envoys. They refused our offers of protection in the plague years, and when the plague came, they bled. They are a stiff-necked, sentimental, self-regarding family of cooks and farmers, and they have survived this season by the grace of our Wall, and we have given them everything." He looks at her. "I would like to know what we are asking in return."

"Nothing."

"Then I cannot support you."

"Elder."

"I will not vote to starve our own pupils for the pride of the Garden." His eyes are hard. "It is not that I do not grieve. I do. I have buried four hundred. But I did not bury them so that our granaries could be opened to strangers."

"They are not strangers," says Shan, suddenly, from the foot. He flushes at his own boldness, but he goes on. "Forgive me. But Elder Gu died for the Wall. Lan Wen died on it. We stood on the same stone for five days. If we are not allies after that, I do not know what the word means."

"They are allies when it suits them."

"They are alive, Elder Mu. That seems to me to suit everyone."

A murmur. Mu's mouth thins. Han lets them argue. She sits down at last, in her own chair, and puts her chin on her fist, and thinks about a bowl of cold tea, and an old man's hands, and the way he said I would like that very much.

* * *

She does not decide. That is the shameful part.

She leaves the council with the question open, and walks out onto the Wall in the thin blue dark, and stands for an hour at the ninth buttress with her palm against the stone. She knows what she should do. She has known since the granary. But knowing and doing are as far apart as the two ends of the Pass, and she finds that she cannot cross.

Because Mu is right.

That is what galls her. He is right about the tithes. He is right about the plague years. He is right about the stiff-necked Garden and its sentimental, maddening, exasperating pride. She remembers sitting across a table from Zhao, thirty years ago, in a negotiation over water rights, and watching the old woman refuse a perfectly reasonable offer out of what Han could only call contempt. She remembers the charter of the Garden's autonomy, which she herself voted against, as a young Elder, on the grounds that it was impractical. She remembers being told she was cold.

I was, she thinks. I was very cold.

The stone is warm under her hand. It hums, faintly, a deep slow thrum that she can feel up through her wrist. It is the keystone, the array that Gu gave his life for. She has never listened to it before. She listens now, with her eyes closed, and under the hum she hears something else: a pattern, regular, almost a pulse. It rises and falls. It rises and falls.

She opens her eyes.

At the foot of the buttress, set into the dressed stone at head height, there is a small plaque. It is new, the character burned only two weeks ago. Gu, the Eighth. Beneath it, in Lu Fei's neat hand, are the words she dictated at dawn on the sixth day, before she could think better of them.

He said he would be in good company.

She touches the lettering. She does not know what she expects. A voice, a sign, a flicker of light. There is nothing. There is only the stone, and the wind, and the sound of her own heart, and she thinks, with a clear, sad lack of surprise: He would have laughed at me.

You will be a good Head, he said. You always ask.

"Uncle," she says, aloud. "I don't know what to do."

The ninth Weight, hanging at its post on the parapet, gives a single, soft swing.

* * *

Lu Fei finds her in the small hours, still on the Wall, and he is not alone.

There is someone with him. A tall figure in a gray cloak, wrapped against the cold, with a staff and a pack and the stiff unhurried bearing of a messenger who has ridden far. Han turns. The lantern light falls across a lean tired face, and she knows it, and her mouth goes dry.

"Captain Sera," she says.

"Head Han." The girl bows. She is very young, and very proud, and covered in road dust. "I rode through the night. I hope you will forgive the hour."

"You are the Garden's envoy?"

"I am its Captain. The Clan Head sent me. She said..." Sera hesitates. "She said not to bring a petition. She said you would find it insulting."

"Did she."

"She said you would find it insulting, and that you would be right." A small, rueful twitch of the mouth. "She sent me with a different message."

Han waits.

"The Clan Head says that she wrote you a letter at the fourth hour, and that she regrets it." Sera takes a breath. "She says it was a coward's letter. It stated the Garden's numbers and left the Sect to draw the conclusion, which is the way her mother's generation asked for favors, and she is ashamed of it. She asks me to say that the Garden will not starve. It has Qinghe. It has a Core that feeds on appetite and gives it back. It will ration by the bowl and eat the roots of its own orchard before it begs. But she says..." The girl's voice wavers. "She says that if the Sect should choose to give, the Garden will not refuse. And that it would not forget."

Han is silent.

"She also says," Sera adds, "that she has been wrong about the Sect for sixty years, and would like to be told so, in person, over tea."

A long pause. The wind turns. On the parapet, the Weights tremble together on their cords, and for a moment, she hears something that sounds almost like a laugh.

"Captain," says Han slowly. "Did Zhao say anything else?"

"She said you would know what to do."

"She is a liar."

"She said you'd say that, too."

Han presses the heel of her hand to her eyes. She stands there a moment, in the cold, with the whole weight of the Wall at her back and the weight of the twelve chairs in her chest. And then, abruptly, she begins to laugh.

It is a terrible sound. It comes out cracked and rusty, and she bends double with it, and cannot stop. Sera stares. Lu Fei looks alarmed. But the laughter goes on, and goes on, and slowly, as it goes, something in her loosens. Something that has been clenched since the first night. The pressure behind her sternum. The ache behind her eyes.

You always ask, she thinks. I always ask.

"Sera," she says, wiping her face. "Sit down. I have a proposal."

* * *

Sera sleeps for three hours on a bench in the Gate tower, and when she wakes, Han is sitting beside her with a cup.

It is not the tea with the heron. It is a plainer cup, chipped, brown, and the tea in it is the cheap rough stuff that the pupils drink on the Wall at midnight. Han holds it out. Sera takes it with both hands and sips, and makes a small startled face.

"Is it supposed to taste of smoke?"

"It tastes of the Wall."

"I see." The girl drinks. Her fingers are trembling. "I'm sorry. I fell asleep."

"You rode eleven miles in the dark, through a field of dead beasts. You may sleep where you like." Han watches her. "Captain Sera. May I ask you something?"

"Of course."

"Lan Wen chose you."

"She did."

"Why?"

Sera frowns into her cup. She is silent so long that Han thinks she will not answer. When she does, her voice is thoughtful, and very young.

"I used to ask her what things looked like," she says. "On the first night. She was blind, you know, and I was her eyes, so I would tell her what I saw. The sky. The Wall. The lamps. And I noticed that after a while she stopped asking what and started asking how. She'd say, How does the line hold? How are the guards standing? And I realized she was teaching me. Not to see. To read."

"Read what?"

"The way a thing stands when it is about to break." Sera looks up. "She said it was the only skill a captain needs. Everything else is only footwork."

Han almost smiles. It is a small, unaccustomed movement, and her face aches with it.

"She was right," she says.

"She was usually right. It was very annoying." The girl takes another swallow. "I don't think I'll be as good."

"No," says Han. "You will be better. You will have the advantage of not being blind."

Sera laughs, startled, and the tension in her narrow shoulders eases for the first time in a week. Then she ducks her head, and her shoulders shake, and Han leaves her to it with the cup, and goes out to the parapet to look at the stars.

* * *

She tells the Elders at dawn, and she tells them everything.

The council chamber is gray with early light, and the eleven faces around the table are gray with it too. She does not stand this time. She sits, with her hands folded, and speaks in a plain clear voice, the way Gu used to teach it: say the true thing first, and the reasons after.

"I am going to give the Garden twelve thousand measures," she says. "I am going to give it today. I am going to send the first convoy before noon."

A stir.

"I am not doing it out of sentiment. I am doing it for three reasons." She holds up a finger. "The first is that we cannot hold the Wall without them. Lan Wen's guards stood on sections one and two for five days, and when the Riders came, it was the Garden that bled for it. If we leave them hungry, we lose them. If we lose them, we lose the corner, and the corner is a door."

A second finger.

"The second is that the Wall is dying. Not now. Not this winter. But Lu Fei's readings are clear. Sections three and five are failing, slowly, from the same limestone rot that took nine. We lost one keystone to hold one section. We will lose seven more by spring. I have been trying to think of how to replace them, and I have come to one conclusion." She looks up the table. "We need a Keeper."

"A Keeper of Walls," says Shan, softly.

"The old title. Created by the Founders. The one who walks the Wall, and reads its arrays, and mends what the stone cannot mend." Han draws a breath. "It has been vacant for four hundred years, because the Sect decided no one living was worthy. I think we have been wrong."

"You mean Lin Jian."

"I do."

Silence.

"He has a Core," she says. "A new one, taken from a dead Alpha. He can fold through stone. He can read an array in the time it takes me to drink a cup of tea. He has spent his whole life standing between this world and something worse." Her voice catches. "And he is dying. He will be dead before the thaw. I am asking the Sect to offer a title to a man with eleven weeks to live."

"Then why?" says Mu. It is not rhetorical. He leans forward, with narrowed eyes. "Why bother, Head? He cannot hold it. He cannot mend what is broken. What does a dying man's name add to a wall?"

"It adds everything." She turns to him. "Elder, you know the oldest rule. A Keeper's name is written into the array. It becomes the keystone's second key. When the Keeper dies, the name remains. The Wall remembers. It does not need him alive. It needs him named."

Mu goes quite still.

"Gu gave us the first keystone," she says. "We write his name on the buttress and feel it hold. Lin Jian can give us the second. He will write his name on all eight sections, in his own hand, with his own Core, and when he is gone, the Wall will carry it. He will be the Wall, Elder. In every stone."

"At what cost?"

"I do not know." She is honest. "I have asked Lu Fei. He says the Seat will bind him. He will not be able to leave the Pass after he accepts. He will walk the Wall until he cannot walk, and then he will sit on it."

"And the Garden?"

"The Garden will have to send its Keeper to the Sect." She meets his eyes. "I know what that means. I know what I am asking. A dying man who belongs to them, and who they will lose twice. But I think he would choose it. I think he is a man who would rather be useful than comfortable."

Mu does not answer.

"That is the second reason," she says quietly. "And the third is the simplest." She looks down the table at the empty chair, the cold tea, the faded heron. "Gu asked me for tea. I gave it to him. I have never been so glad of anything in my life. I would like, just once, to do the same for someone who is still alive."

* * *

The vote is taken at noon, and it is not unanimous.

Shan raises his hand first, and then the archivist Ro, and then one by one, haltingly, the others. Pei lifts her stump. Eight. Nine. Ten.

Mu does not.

He sits at her right with his hands folded, white-faced, rigid. He does not look at her. He does not look at anyone. When the vote is counted, and the tenth hand lowered, and the silence has stretched to breaking, he rises, with the slow deliberation of an old man leaving a dinner table.

"I will not pretend to approve," he says.

"No one asks you to."

"I will not obstruct. I have taken the oath." He bows, a curt stiff bow. "But I will not remain, Head, at a table that gives away our bread to those who have never given us theirs. I will take my leave of the Seat."

"Elder—"

"Forty of my pupils are of my mind." His face does not change. "I shall be at the old hermitage on the north ridge. If the Sect has need of me, it may send. If not, I shall pray for it."

He walks to the door. Han stands, half-risen, with her hand extended. She cannot find the words. She wants to say stay, and forgive me, and you were right about the tithes. She wants to say a great many things, and none of them is any use.

At the door he stops. He does not turn.

"Gu would have done the same," he says, quite softly. "I will say that. He would have done exactly the same." A long pause. "That does not make it wise."

He goes out.

For a time nobody speaks. The dust drifts in the gray light. Somewhere beyond the walls, in the courtyard, a pupil is calling to another about water.

Then Sera, who has been standing in the corner with her cap in her fist, clears her throat.

"Head Han," she says. "The first cart?"

"Within the hour." Han sits down. Her legs have gone suddenly weak. "Lu Fei. Write the Seat of Keeper. Plain script. Plain words. It is to be delivered by hand."

"To whom?"

"To the Clan Head. She will know how to put it to him." Han presses her palms to her eyes. "And Lu Fei."

"Head?"

"After that, send for a bowl of tea. A proper one. With the heron."

He nods. He goes out, and Sera follows. And she is left alone in the long bare chamber, with ten empty chairs and one full one, and the cold gray light, and the dull knowledge, settling slowly into her bones, that she has just done the right thing at the price of losing a friend.

She sits very still.

Outside, on the Wall, the bell begins to ring.
